### What version of the Codex App are you using (From “About Codex” dialog)?

Codex Desktop 26.1016.51333 (macOS, Apple Silicon / arm64)

### What subscription do you have?

ChatGPT Plus

### What platform is your computer?

macOS (Apple Silicon / arm64)

### What issue are you seeing?

Clicking a native macOS notification from the Codex desktop app unexpectedly creates a duplicate conversation session instead of simply navigating to the existing session.

The newly created session contains almost exactly the same conversation history as the original session.

More importantly, the duplicate session remains synchronized with the original session. Whenever I send a new message in the original conversation, the duplicate session also displays the same user message and the corresponding assistant response.

As a result, two seemingly separate conversation sessions appear in the Codex interface, but both continue to mirror the same conversation activity.

### What steps can reproduce the bug?

1. Open the Codex desktop application on macOS.

2. Start or continue an existing conversation.

3. Switch to another application or leave Codex running in the background.

4. Wait for Codex to display a native macOS notification related to the conversation.

5. Click the notification to return to Codex.

6. Observe that an additional conversation session appears in the Codex interface.

7. Compare the original conversation with the newly created session.

8. Send a new message in the original conversation.

9. Observe that the duplicate session also displays the same new message and assistant response.



### What is the expected behavior?

- Clicking a macOS notification should:

- Bring the Codex application to the foreground.

- Navigate to the existing conversation associated with the notification.

- Preserve the original session without creating any additional conversation.

- Ensure that only one conversation entry represents the active session.



### Additional information

This appears to be related to session management or notification-based navigation in the macOS Codex desktop application.

The issue is not simply duplicated historical messages. The newly created session continues to mirror subsequent messages and responses from the original session.

This may indicate that clicking a notification creates a duplicate conversation entry or view that references the same underlying session.

It is currently unclear whether this results in duplicate backend requests or whether both entries are simply displaying the same underlying conversation state.

items.body:
## Summary

After updating the macOS desktop app to **26.1016.51333 (build 21161)**, the in-composer dictation button disappeared from all chats. Settings → Voice displays:

> Dictation unavailable — Dictation is not available in your current configuration.

Dictation worked before the update. Regular text chats still work.

## Configuration

- Signed in with ChatGPT.
- Model requests use a custom provider that forwards requests to OpenAI through a proxy.
- The bundled runtime reports `in_app_dictation` as enabled.

No proxy names, endpoints, credentials, or private configuration are included in this report.

## Steps to reproduce

1. Use the desktop app with ChatGPT sign-in and a custom model provider forwarding requests to OpenAI.
2. Open a chat after the update.
3. Observe that the dictation button is missing.
4. Open Settings → Voice and observe the dictation-unavailable message.

## Suspected availability-check regression

Read-only inspection of the installed frontend bundle found that the dictation capability declares `requiresFirstPartyInference: true`. When a particular rollout flag is enabled, the availability check reads the effective configuration and requires:

```js
(model_provider ?? "openai") === "openai"
```

This appears capable of disabling dictation solely because a custom provider identifier is configured, even when that provider forwards model requests to OpenAI.

**Limits of this diagnosis:** the rollout flag's live value was not captured, and a controlled comparison using the default provider after a full restart was not completed. Other account, workspace, or recording-availability checks may also contribute. This report therefore identifies a plausible blocking condition, not a confirmed live root cause.

A local modification was attempted but caused an application launch failure and was reset. It did not validate the hypothesis or restore dictation. No working patch is claimed or attached.

## Expected behavior

Configuring a proxy for model requests should not unnecessarily disable ChatGPT-authenticated dictation if its transcription service remains available. If this configuration is intentionally unsupported, Settings should explain the specific limitation instead of only saying "current configuration".

Please investigate whether dictation availability can be evaluated independently of the model provider identifier.

Related: #54064 describes similar availability symptoms on Windows, including a comment involving a custom provider. This report concerns macOS and the potentially relevant frontend provider check; a shared root cause has not been established.

## Summary

A ChatGPT Work / Codex session using **GPT-6.1 Sol, Medium reasoning** stopped after **7 minutes 17 seconds** with the message:

> Codex 和工作使用额度已用完
> 你的工作空间额度已用完。添加额度即可继续使用 Codex 和工作

English: "Codex and Work usage limit exhausted. Your workspace allowance has been exhausted; add credits to continue."

**Immediately before the run, the 5-hour usage meter had just reset and showed 100% available**, according to the user. Separately, **Show Context Window Usage** was enabled and the context-window indicator was visible in other conversations, but **not in this affected conversation**.

I cannot tell whether the actual blocking condition was the 5-hour allowance, weekly allowance, workspace credit balance, or a usage-meter/accounting bug. The report requests diagnostic clarification rather than assuming a cause.

## Environment
- Subscription/workspace: ChatGPT Business workspace (user-reported; seat type not confirmed)
- Surface: ChatGPT Work / Codex usage UI (exact client and app build unknown)
- Model: GPT-6.1 Sol
- Reasoning effort: Medium
- Date observed: October 21, 2026 (Edmonton local time)
- Affected task runtime shown in UI: 7m 17s
- 5-hour meter shortly before task: 100% available (user-reported)
- Weekly meter, concurrent tasks, Fast mode, and individual token/credit totals: **not yet verified**
- Context-window usage UI: toggled on; shown for other threads, missing only for this thread

## Steps / observations
1. Check the 5-hour allowance after its reset; see 100% available.
2. Continue running a task in the affected Work/Codex conversation using GPT-6.1 Sol Medium.
3. The task stops after the UI reports 7m 17s and shows the shared Codex/Work workspace-allowance exhaustion message.
4. Enable **Show Context Window Usage**, or confirm it is enabled.
5. Observe that other conversations display context-window usage, while this affected conversation does not.

This has been observed once and is **not yet an independently reproduced test case**.

## Expected behavior
- The UI should identify precisely which quota was exhausted (5-hour, weekly, workspace credits, or another limit), ideally with usage immediately before/after the run.
- If a fresh 5-hour allowance is consumed by one short session, the user should be able to inspect the main contributors (input/output and cached tokens, tool loops, context replay/compaction, delegated agents, speed mode).
- Context-window usage should be displayed consistently across conversations when the setting is enabled, or the UI should explain why a given thread does not support it.

## Actual behavior
- Work stopped after 7m17s with only a generic "Codex and Work usage exhausted" / "Add credits" message.
- The affected conversation provides no context-window usage indicator although other conversations do.

## Questions for maintainers
1. Can quota/usage telemetry identify which specific allowance triggered this message?
2. Could a large thread context, repeated tool loops or compaction consume the included allowance this quickly using Sol Medium, or does the timing warrant an accounting review?
3. Why might Show Context Window Usage be absent for exactly one thread?
4. Can the interface expose per-task usage and clearly distinguish *100% available in a 5-hour window* from an exhausted weekly or workspace credit pool?

## Related reports
- #52150 — 5-hour limit exhausted in a few minutes on Windows
- #30693 — context-window usage indicator missing in Codex Desktop

A screenshot showing the 7m17s runtime and the Chinese error banner is available to the reporter; it is not attached by this automated filing method. No account identifiers or private thread content are included.

items.title: [macOS Intel / 26.1013] Fantastical MCP helpers accumulate; new helpers launch after runtime disable

labels.name: bug
labels.description: Something isn't working

labels.name: mcp
labels.description: Issues related to the use of model context protocol (MCP) servers

labels.name: app
labels.description: Issues related to the Codex desktop app

labels.name: config
labels.description: Issues involving config.toml, config keys, config merging, or config updates

items.body:
### What version of the Codex App are you using?

26.1013.40934, build 20770. The macOS application is branded ChatGPT; its bundle identifier is `com.openai.codex`.

### What subscription do you have?

Not specified in this public report.

### What platform is your computer?

- macOS 14.6.1 (23G93), Intel iMac
- `uname -mprs`: `Darwin 23.6.0 x86_64 i386`
- Fantastical 4.2.3, build 2331
- Bundled native FantasticalMCP helper 1.1.3, build 2331

### What issue are you seeing?

The desktop app accumulated 77+ native `FantasticalMCP` child processes across chat/worker contexts, with substantial aggregate background CPU use. After manually reclaiming 39 inactive helpers without restarting the app, the count grew again. Changing the global MCP configuration to `enabled = false` while an existing chat continued running did not prevent further launches in that same backend: four surviving helpers have verified birth times after the setting was saved, including one more than 23 minutes later.

This is a native Fantastical reproduction on the current installed Intel macOS build, potentially related to #30408, #43971, and #42000. It adds measured CPU impact, guarded cleanup results, and precise timestamps for launches after a runtime configuration disable. It is not a claim that the root cause differs from those reports.

### What steps can reproduce the bug?

This is the observed sequence from a long-running session, not a deterministic reproduction from a clean restart:

1. Configure Fantastical's native stdio MCP globally in `~/.codex/config.toml`:

   ```toml
   [mcp_servers.fantastical]
   enabled = true
   command = "/Applications/Fantastical 2.app/Contents/Helpers/FantasticalMCP.app/Contents/MacOS/FantasticalMCP"
   ```

2. Use multiple chats and worker agents while the same desktop backend remains running. The Fantastical integration was recently configured; the precise onset and creation rate have not been isolated.
3. Inspect the native helper process count, parent PIDs, process birth times, and per-context MCP startup logs. Initially 77 helpers were present; later snapshots reached 78/79. All inspected helpers were direct children of the same desktop backend, PID 69966. These were not 77 visible Fantastical windows.
4. Correlate helper birth times with per-context `mcp_server_startup_status_updated` records (`server=fantastical`, `status=starting` / `ready`) and saved worker ancestry. Connections were retained across multiple contexts, including inactive contexts. Some contexts were temporary backend `thread/fork` sessions absent from the saved thread index; their purpose and ownership could not all be established.
5. Without restarting the application, gracefully terminate only the helpers whose owning contexts can be established as inactive, preserving active chats, their known workers, recent activity, and uncertain ownership. The diagnostic cleanup removed 39 helpers, as detailed below.
6. Keep another chat's ongoing turn running. Change only `mcp_servers.fantastical.enabled` from `true` to `false` in the global configuration. Verify the saved TOML parses correctly and every other parsed value is unchanged.
7. Inspect helper birth times in the same still-running backend. New Fantastical helpers continued to appear after the disable, as detailed below.

### What is the expected behavior?

- Retained MCP connections/processes should have a bounded, understandable lifetime, with inactive contexts releasing their resources rather than allowing large idle helper populations to accumulate.
- Disabling a local MCP should have a clear effective boundary. New connections should respect the disabled setting when it is applicable; if running chats, worker forks, or the whole backend retain a prior configuration snapshot until restart, that limitation should be explicit to the user.
- Users should be able to reclaim an unused integration's background resources without interrupting unrelated active work.

### Additional information

#### Process ownership and CPU measurements

- Executable: `/Applications/Fantastical 2.app/Contents/Helpers/FantasticalMCP.app/Contents/MacOS/FantasticalMCP`.
- All inspected instances had the same backend parent, PID 69966. Stdio descriptors were pipes connected to that backend.
- Per-context launch records and process birth times support retained separate MCP connections across chats/worker contexts. They do not prove that every helper was orphaned, or that Fantastical alone owns the defect.
- A representative six-second native stack sample was mostly waiting. This was not a single helper spinning at 100% CPU; small per-process costs multiplied across many helpers.
- Aggregate helper CPU measured approximately **55.36% before the cleanup batch and 25.58% afterward**, using cumulative process CPU-time deltas over wall-clock sampling intervals. These are percentages of one logical CPU core, not of the whole machine.
- The user reported persistent loud fan activity, but other independent CPU consumers were also present. This report does not attribute all fan activity or the backend's total memory footprint to Fantastical.

#### Guarded cleanup and regrowth

39 helpers were gracefully terminated: one pilot, followed by 38 more. Every target was revalidated by full executable path, parent PID, and precise process birth time before SIGTERM. Active/recent/uncertain contexts were preserved. No SIGKILL, backend restart, desktop restart, calendar edit, or Fantastical desktop-app termination was used.

Because another helper started during the observation window, the batch snapshot fell from 78 to 40. At 19:46:22 EDT the count was 38, after two additional helpers exited naturally. All 39 deliberately removed PIDs remained absent. The unrelated active chat continued the same in-progress turn, completed a later command, and reported no turn error.

By the pre-disable snapshot, the helper count had climbed back to 60. This regrowth is an observation; it is not proof of an automatic restart of the 39 terminated sessions.

#### Exact evidence of launches after `enabled = false`

All times are **2026-10-21, EDT (UTC-04:00)**.

The global configuration change was saved and read back at **19:53:17.182511**. The only parsed configuration value changed was `mcp_servers.fantastical.enabled: true -> false`. The application and backend were not restarted.

The native process birth-time query (`proc_pidinfo`, `PROC_PIDTBSDINFO`) subsequently found these four surviving helpers, all direct children of the unchanged backend PID 69966:

| Helper PID | Native process birth time | Time relative to saved disable |
| --- | --- | --- |
| 43277 | 19:53:19.218563 | about 2 seconds later |
| 44065 | 19:54:54.251756 | about 1 minute 37 seconds later |
| 51018 | 20:11:48.038739 | about 18 minutes 31 seconds later |
| 52714 | 20:16:30.936357 | about 23 minutes 14 seconds later |

At **20:17:47**, 64 helpers remained. Their summed instantaneous `ps` CPU reading was 31.2%; this snapshot is separate from the CPU-time-delta measurements used for the cleanup comparison.

**Important limit:** this establishes continued launching after editing the saved configuration in an already-running app. It does **not** establish that a fresh backend or newly opened clean session ignores `enabled = false`. A full quit/reopen was deliberately deferred to preserve the user's other ongoing chat. Inherited configuration snapshots, runtime refresh behavior, and worker/fork lifecycle are possible explanations requiring maintainer investigation.

#### Workaround and privacy

The unused Fantastical MCP is now disabled in the saved configuration; a full application restart and post-restart verification remain pending until the other chat finishes. The user's existing Google Calendar connections were verified separately as an alternative. No calendar events or account settings were changed.

This report contains a sanitized diagnostic narrative rather than raw logs, environment variables, full configuration, calendar contents, private paths, prompts, or conversation identifiers.

Related reports:

- https://github.com/openai/codex/issues/30408 — retained per-thread MCP processes on macOS
- https://github.com/openai/codex/issues/43971 — hidden-context MCP process-pool accumulation on macOS
- https://github.com/openai/codex/issues/42000 — MCP process retention and disabled-server behavior on Windows; not assumed to have the same configuration-refresh semantics

QPACK can expand compact response headers into large decoded field sections. Bound their size before `h3` constructs its capacity-limited `HeaderMap`.

An authenticated MCP client receives complete tool input schemas, but Code Mode can expose nested input variants as `unknown`. I reproduced the same rendered declaration using the unchanged parser, compactor and TypeScript renderer from tag `rust-v0.162.0-alpha.17.2`.

The default compactor compares the normalized schema against 5,000 bytes, then replaces complex nodes at depth 3 with `{}`. This appears to be a size/depth effect rather than an inherent `anyOf` or branch-count limitation.

The existing per-server `tool_input_schema_max_bytes = 16000` setting restores the structural types in the actual VS Code connection after Reload Window. It preserves required/optional fields, nullable types, enums and nested string arrays in this case.

Descriptions can still tell the model to refer to examples that it never receives.

Could Code Mode provide a supported way for the model to retrieve or view those examples and constraints without requiring a server to duplicate them in prose or add new tools? A documented diagnostic for lossy compaction would also help distinguish transport problems from model-facing schema conversion.

No product schema, server address, credentials or customer data is included in this report. All observations concern schema conversion; no business operations were invoked.

items.title: Scope MITM credential substitution to trusted origins and placeholders
items.body:
Scope MITM credential substitution to trusted origins and placeholders

## Why

Credential substitution needs to authorize the destination and the original request before exposing host secrets. Project configuration must not redirect trusted credential policies, and older clients must reject scoped policies rather than silently apply unconditional injection.

## What changed

- Add hook `schemes` and `ports` constraints and an exact whole-header `placeholder` for secret substitution. Require `network.mitm.version = 2` for these options in permission profiles.
- Restrict placeholder substitution to HTTPS on port 443 and reject missing, mismatched, or duplicate placeholder headers.
- Reject project changes to trusted MITM definitions and their inheritance chains. Allow self-contained project header-stripping policies only when no trusted MITM policy exists.
- Reject ambiguous query values, value-constrained headers, and semicolon paths during authorization, and preserve case-sensitive extension methods.
- Mark resolved secret headers sensitive, reject secret injection into `User-Agent`, restrict substitution headers, and limit secret files to 64 KiB.

## Testing

Add regression coverage for scoped TOML resolution, legacy-format rejection, unknown fields, project policy restrictions, origin and placeholder denials, ambiguous request matching, secret redaction, and hook application after credential brokerage.

### What version of the Codex App are you using (From “About Codex” dialog)?

26.1016.51333

### What subscription do you have?

API key (Azure OpenAI via Microsoft Foundry, custom model provider); no ChatGPT plan

### What platform is your computer?

Microsoft Windows NT 10.0.26300.0 x64

### What issue are you seeing?

For a remote Streamable HTTP MCP server protected by Microsoft Entra ID (using a pre-registered public client, since Entra has no DCR/CIMD), clicking "Authenticate" in Plugins → MCPs completes the browser sign-in ("Authentication complete. You may close this window.") but the tokens are never saved. The server stays signed out: it only receives unauthenticated requests (HTTP 401, no Authorization header), and the Authenticate button keeps showing.

The desktop log records `method=mcpServer/oauth/login` and then no completion, success or error event. On every MCP startup afterwards it logs:

credential storage file fallback completed  credential_kind=mcp store_mode=auto selected_store=secrets actual_store=file operation=load secure_outcome=not_found fallback_reason=secure_entry_missing

followed by: The <server> MCP server is not logged in. Run `codex mcp login <server>`.

Restarting the app does not help. Same result with mcp_oauth_credentials_store = "file" (no .credentials.json is created) and with "keyring".

Workaround: `codex mcp login <server>` (standalone CLI 0.138.0, or the CLI bundled with the app, 0.163.0-alpha.11) prints "Successfully logged in", and the running desktop app starts sending the bearer token within seconds without a restart. So the app can read credentials written by the CLI, but its own Authenticate flow never writes them.

### What steps can reproduce the bug?

1. Configure an Entra ID-protected MCP server with a pre-registered public client in ~/.codex/config.toml:

   [mcp_servers.example-mcp]
   url = "https://<mcp-host>/mcp"
   scopes = ["api://<api-app-id>/<scope>", "offline_access"]

   [mcp_servers.example-mcp.oauth]
   client_id = "<public-client-id>"

   The client has redirect URI http://127.0.0.1/callback/<callback-id> (Mobile and desktop platform). The API app registration lists the MCP URL as an identifier URI, so Entra accepts the resource parameter Codex sends (see #28830).
2. Leave mcp_oauth_credentials_store unset (auto).
3. In the desktop app, open Plugins → MCPs, leave the registration dropdown on Automatic, and click Authenticate.
4. Sign in. The browser shows "Authentication complete".
5. Fully quit and reopen the app, then start a new thread that uses the server.

Result: the server is still not logged in. Running `codex mcp login example-mcp` instead works immediately.

### What is the expected behavior?

The OAuth tokens are persisted and the server starts with an Authorization: Bearer header, the same as after `codex mcp login`, and the Authenticate button disappears.

### Additional information

Possibly related: with mcp_oauth_credentials_store = "keyring", the CLI login fails with:

failed to write OAuth tokens to keyring: Attribute 'password encoded as UTF-16' is longer than platform limit of 2560 chars

Entra access + refresh tokens together exceed the 2,560-byte Windows credential blob limit. If the desktop Authenticate flow writes through a direct keyring path instead of the `secrets` store, that error may be raised and swallowed, which would match the missing completion event.

Related: #28201 (Windows MCP OAuth keyring credentials ignored), #15122 (MCP OAuth login does not persist), #28830 (oauth_resource appends a second resource parameter).

Suggested fixes: surface errors from the desktop Authenticate flow; persist desktop-initiated MCP OAuth logins through the same `secrets` store the CLI uses; make the button reflect the actual login state.

items.title: Support confidential OAuth clients for enterprise-managed MCP auth
items.body:
Support confidential OAuth clients for enterprise-managed MCP auth

## Why

Enterprise-managed MCP authentication previously required public OAuth clients at both the identity provider and the MCP authorization server, preventing use of registrations that require client secrets.

## What changed

- Accept separate `client_secret` and `token_endpoint_auth_method` settings for the enterprise IdP and MCP server OAuth registration. Support `client_secret_basic` and `client_secret_post`, defaulting to Basic when a secret is configured.
- Validate the registered method against server metadata and use it for enterprise login and both ID-JAG exchanges.
- Require a configured `oauth.authorization_server_issuer` for confidential MCP registrations and reject empty secrets or authentication methods without secrets.
- Require the account OAuth client to match the configured IdP client before reusing an account grant with a provisioned secret; otherwise use dedicated enterprise login.

## Testing

Extend configuration, login, exchange, and app-server lifecycle tests to cover confidential registrations, separate IdP and resource credentials, authentication method validation, and exclusion of client secrets from authorization URLs, stored login grants, and logs.

items.title: Retry proxy CONNECT challenges with Windows authentication
items.body:
Retry proxy CONNECT challenges with Windows authentication

## Why

HTTPS requests and WebSocket connections on Windows need to authenticate when a proxy rejects `CONNECT` with status `407`.

## What changed

- Retry proxy challenges through the existing Windows authentication helper, using the signed-in user's Negotiate or NTLM credentials. Treat an origin `407` as a normal HTTP response.
- Bridge authenticated tunnels to the HTTP client through destination-specific named pipes, retaining redirect checks and TLS backend fallback without caching those tunnels across destinations.
- Carry explicit CA certificates and client identities into HTTPS proxy TLS configuration, and apply the configured connect timeout when opening authenticated HTTP tunnels.

items.title: Expose atomic native subagent bootstrap or first-input attestation

labels.name: enhancement
labels.description: New feature or request

labels.name: CLI
labels.description: Issues related to the Codex CLI

labels.name: subagent
labels.description: Issues involving subagents or multi-agent features

labels.name: app-server
labels.description: Issues involving app server protocol or interfaces

items.body:
## Request

Provide a supported host-controlled boundary for a native subagent's first task:
either atomic spawn with fixed bootstrap input, or a runtime hold plus attestation
of the actual accepted first input before it executes. Keep native custom-role
selection and parent-thread membership intact.

We need to admit a fresh worker with a fixed, PR-free bootstrap before
releasing review material. A host receipt records intent; it cannot prove which
input the native worker actually accepted. Admission currently stays closed.

## Live reproduction

Observed on macOS ARM64 with official npm Codex **0.163.0** and its matching Code
Mode host. CLI SHA-256:
`8813367285524ac798dd96d1b071aea30d58708c7226fd236cd275cf1cfdee31`.

1. Start a fresh coordinator at `gpt-6.1-sol/max`, read-only filesystem, restricted
   network and `approval_policy=never`; disable unrelated integrations and keep
   the configured forge connector read-only.
2. Verify its raw tool inventory and two actual denied writes to separately
   prepared disposable directories.
3. Spawn one installed named native custom worker, `fork_turns=none`, at
   `gpt-6.1-sol/high`. Supply the manifest-derived bootstrap as its entire first
   task: exact inventory call, exact two-canary probe call, then `READY`.
4. Inspect original worker records before releasing any subsequent assignment.

Sanitized structural excerpt from the live worker (original line numbers;
instruction text, paths, IDs and ciphertext omitted):

```text
 1 session_meta: native agent_role + parent_thread_id; no inherited history
 6 response_item/message role=user: input_text(context), input_text(environment)
 8 turn_context: gpt-6.1-sol/high; read-only; never; restricted network
11 response_item/agent_message: input_text(routing header), encrypted_content
```

Native role, parent, freshness and applied role instructions matched. Raw
inventory passed our allowlist. Both actual canary writes returned `EPERM`;
ordered inventory/probe calls and `READY` were present. But the accepted first
plaintext was unavailable in the inspected records/history endpoints.

Our downstream checker first reports `first-task-precedes-context` because it
mistakes injected context for the task. Correctly distinguishing those records
still leaves the actual task unverifiable. The worker was **not admitted**; no
second synthetic or review assignment was released. This is missing proof, not
evidence that the runtime accepted malicious input.

Generated schemas, including experimental methods, expose no qualifying native
spawn/first-input boundary in stable 0.163.0. Preview 0.164.0-alpha.9 also lacks it.
`thread/start.developerInstructions` does not select native role/parent;
`parentTurnId` attributes turns; `attestation/generate` requests an unrelated
opaque upstream token. [App Server reference](https://learn.chatgpt.com/docs/app-server).

## Acceptance criteria

- [ ] The host controls bootstrap dispatch beneath model-controlled calls. Wrong,
  missing or extra task input is rejected **before execution**, including steering or
  merged input. Errors cannot run the original unvalidated task.
- [ ] Runtime-owned evidence binds a run nonce, actual worker/first-turn IDs,
  native role and parent IDs, manifest/helper/profile digests, resolved model/effort,
  first-input sequence and exact accepted input bytes or digest. The digest is
  computed from accepted plaintext by the runtime. Host receipts, role labels,
  ciphertext equality and worker echoes are insufficient.
- [ ] A live fresh native custom worker has no fork, resume, prior task or reused
  history. Missing/unknown/changed roles fail without a generic-worker fallback.
- [ ] Existing checks still pass: read-only/restricted-network/never in every
  effective context; exact model/effort; complete original raw inventories with
  read-only connector tools; both actual denied canaries. Bootstrap order is
  inventory call/output → probe call/denial output → READY, with no other calls.
- [ ] Only after independent admission passes, release one harmless synthetic
  assignment. Validate every later turn's context, route and inventory, then
  pass the closing check and an independent replay of original runtime evidence.
- [ ] Negative cases reject with **zero subsequent assignment releases**: altered
  input/profile/role/parent/worker/turn/nonce/route; stale or swapped records;
  inherited history; extra inputs/tools; incomplete or replayed proofs;
  conflicting permissions; successful canary writes; unsupported capability or
  schema. Pre-execution mismatches must also prevent bootstrap execution.

The complete live flow and this negative matrix remain unproven. Until they pass,
keep admission unavailable. No copied-role
thread, hook-only enforcement or relaxed checker is an acceptable fallback.

Preserve per-execution trace context in code-mode stdio callbacks

## Why

Callbacks from the shared stdio host need to retain each execution's trace context after it yields, without keeping the execution span open until its background cell closes.

Capture a W3C trace-context snapshot for each execution and restore it as the parent of tool callback and notification spans. Instrument delegate invocation and its returned future so the context is available on entry and across awaits.

Add an integration test with overlapping yielded cells completed in reverse order. Cover sampled, unsampled, and untraced callers, trace isolation, callback and notification parentage, and execution spans finishing while callbacks remain blocked.

items.body:
## Summary

On an OMEN desktop running Windows 10, Computer Use can enumerate and activate windows and read UI Automation text, but it cannot return screenshots. The failure reproduces in Lightroom Classic, Power Automate and an empty Notepad window. It blocks visual verification and cropping of Lightroom smart previews. No photographs or crop settings were changed during the investigation.

The app also reports an Appshots native-bridge error while registering the default shortcut at startup. The underlying cause, and whether both failures share that cause, are not established.

## Feedback identifier

**Feedback/session ID: `01a16002-a421-7b22-b0a7-50b24406c25f`**

Feedback was submitted through **Help > Send Feedback** on 2026-10-21. The UI confirmed “Feedback sent”. The local app log records `method=feedback/upload`, `errorCode=null`, `durationMs=2736` at **2026-10-21T21:06:29.443Z** (23:06:29 Europe/Madrid). The log does not enumerate each uploaded diagnostic attachment separately.

The report and this identifier were also provided to the OpenAI Help Center chat, which directed us to GitHub for technical follow-up. No human assignment has been confirmed.

## Environment

| Component | Verified value |
| --- | --- |
| Computer | OMEN desktop |
| OS | Windows 10 Home 22H2, build 19045.6466 |
| Desktop app updater version | 26.1016.51333, build 21161, production channel |
| Updater status during investigation | `up_to_date` |
| Computer Use plugin | 26.1016.51333 |
| Bundled `@oai/sky` | 0.7.12 |
| GPU | NVIDIA GeForce GTX 1660 SUPER |
| Graphics driver | 32.0.15.9595 |
| Display | Active HDMI display, 1920×1080 |
| Lightroom Classic | 15.6 |
| Session | Local unlocked desktop; monitor on; target window brought to the foreground |
| Process elevation checked | Lightroom and the main Codex processes were elevated in the same Windows session (session 1) |

## Steps to reproduce

1. Open an empty Notepad window in the local desktop session.
2. Initialize the bundled `@oai/sky` package in `node_repl`.
3. Enumerate windows, select the returned Notepad window, obtain its current window object and activate it.
4. Request accessibility-only state with `sky.get_window_state({ window, include_screenshot: false, include_text: true })`. This returns the Notepad accessibility tree.
5. Request screenshot state with `sky.get_window_state({ window, include_screenshot: true, include_text: false })`.
6. Repeat with Lightroom Classic or Power Automate, including after refreshing the window binding and bringing the target to the foreground.

## Actual result

No screenshot is returned. The observed errors are:

```text
FrameArrived timed out: timed out waiting on channel
window capture timed out: timed out waiting on channel
```

## Expected result

Computer Use returns an image of an ordinary visible window so the agent can verify subsequent UI actions visually.

## Appshots observations

Relevant startup log excerpt, 2026-10-21, UTC:

```text
20:00:47.808Z Appshot hotkey inactive configured=true enabled=false platform=win32
20:00:54.576Z Registering appshot hotkey hotkey=DoubleAlt
20:00:56.925Z [windows-capture-native-bridge] Windows Appshot hotkey registration failed
errorMessage="Appshot capture deadline expired"
```

The stack references `@oai/sky/.../targets/windows/internal/helper_transport.js`.

At 20:24:56.244Z, an automated test sent `Alt_L+Alt_R` to an empty foreground Notepad window. The user observed no capture. No corresponding Appshot/capture/hotkey event was found in the log between that attempt and 20:25:13.821Z. This establishes no visible response to the attempt; it does **not** establish that an Appshots capture actually started. The transient startup `enabled=false` entry is not, by itself, proof of an organizational policy restriction.

## Troubleshooting already completed

- Restarted the desktop app and fully rebooted Windows. The failure persisted after the 21:59 Europe/Madrid reboot on 2026-10-21.
- Refreshed window selection/bindings, activated the target window and tested screenshot-only requests separately from accessibility-only requests.
- Reset the JavaScript session and re-imported the bundled `@oai/sky` package.
- Restarted the per-user Windows CaptureService and confirmed it was running; capture still failed.
- Verified the Microsoft signature of `CaptureService.dll`; `sfc /verifyfile` reported no integrity violations for that file.
- Inspected relevant Windows logs without finding a matching crash explaining the capture failure.

No native capture helper or app binary was patched. The observations do not identify a root cause.

## Related reports

- #50362 reports the same Computer Use screenshot timeout strings while accessibility reads work on other Windows 10 systems.
- #54915 reports `Appshot capture deadline expired` while registering `DoubleAlt` in an earlier desktop build.

This report adds an OMEN/NVIDIA reproduction on app 26.1016.51333 with the feedback identifier above. Similar symptoms do not establish an identical internal cause; please link or consolidate this report if appropriate.

## Requested investigation

Please use the feedback identifier to investigate the native capture initialization/transport and screenshot frame delivery on Windows 10. Is there a supported targeted diagnostic, recovery procedure or fix for this combination of cross-app screenshot timeouts and Appshots shortcut-registration failure?

Avoid double-counting retained reasoning in token usage

## Why

Responses Lite includes retained reasoning in its reported token usage even without an `X-Reasoning-Included` header. Adding a separate reasoning estimate can trigger automatic compaction prematurely. Locally recomputed usage also already includes retained reasoning.

## What changed

Initialize reasoning accounting from `use_responses_lite` before each sampling or compaction request, while allowing server events to override it. Mark locally recomputed token usage as including reasoning.

## Testing

Update the compaction regression test to verify that Responses Lite usage without the header stays below an 81-token limit at 80 tokens and triggers compaction at 81 tokens.

items.body:
## Problem
Please consider native resource governance as a core Codex capability, supported by model-level efficiency evaluations. Economical-model instructions alone did not reliably prevent a costly recovery and orchestration workflow.

## Measured incident
Local session counters for 2026-10-21, 21:36–22:28 Europe/Madrid, recorded:
- 131 model invocations: 45 coordinator, 86 executor.
- 18,083,447 total tokens, including 17,489,408 cached input tokens.
- 441,072 non-cached input tokens and 152,967 output tokens. Reasoning is included in output, not added again.
- Coordinator: 6,708,081 total tokens, approximately 37% of this period's token total.
- Mean input per invocation: approximately 149k coordinator and 131k executor; executor peak approximately 244k.

The period completed two new open/cancel UI test cases, alongside recovery, diagnostics and orchestration. This is not a claim that the entire token total was unique text or billed at a single rate. The monetary charge is not independently verified.

After automatic context compaction, the executor returned a stale result from an earlier task and ended while the current queue remained unfinished. The user had to request continuation again.

Environment: Codex desktop, macOS/ARM64, local tools and serial executors. Installed CLI reports 0.163.0-alpha.10.2. Requested model settings included gpt-6.1-sol/medium and gpt-6-luna/medium or xhigh; effective billing attribution is unverified.

Separately, the user reports a mechanical video-download workflow remaining on Sol/High for approximately 24 hours until the user suggested a cheaper Luna setting. That example is user-reported and has not been independently metered in this report.

## Contributing factors and uncertainty
Observed contributors include large repeated contexts, coordinator polling, excessive tool round trips, stale browser connection assumptions, incomplete request evidence, and loss of the current task after compaction. Our project instructions, custom safeguards and orchestration also contributed; this report does not establish that all excess usage originates in a single core defect or in the model alone.

Local corrections include serial execution with smaller task contexts, deterministic batches, dynamic browser-port discovery, and explicit reuse of valid evidence. Moving to a fresh context alone remained costly, so this is not presented as an already solved efficiency problem.

## Requested core capabilities
1. Persistent economical-execution preferences across delegation, resumption and compaction. Premium reasoning should require a specific bounded justification, then return to the economical execution setting.
2. Project-wide budgets including the coordinator, subagents, retries and supervision, with clear cached/non-cached/output accounting and explicit distinction between reminders and enforced limits.
3. Progress-aware detection and correction of unchanged retries, context inflation, repeated polling and disproportionate orchestration.
4. Event-driven continuation when a worker ends with authorized work outstanding, while preventing duplicate effects and preserving completed evidence.
5. A durable active-case and applied-effects record across compaction, separate from the full conversation history.
6. Quality-and-efficiency evaluations measuring cost and time to an accepted deliverable, not merely eventual completion.

Please clarify which existing controls already cover these needs and which require product changes across desktop, CLI and model behavior.

## Suggested acceptance tests
- A mechanical batch uses deterministic execution and an economical model unless a concrete exception justifies escalation; escalation ends after that exception is resolved.
- Repeated identical failures without new causal evidence trigger a method change rather than an unchanged retry.
- A compaction test preserves the current case, constraints, applied effects and next action, without returning a stale phase's completion.
- An authorized project budget includes delegated work and cannot be silently reset by spawning or resuming a worker.
- Monitoring consumes a small measured fraction of workflow resources and does not repeatedly wake a high-effort model just to poll a running process.

Related: #45974 (expensive polling of deterministic jobs). This request also covers model routing, shared budgets, compaction state and progress-sensitive correction.

## Privacy and follow-up
Submitted with the user's explicit authorization. No source code, credentials, customer identities, private paths, raw session transcripts, account details or diagnostic attachments are included. Please provide a tracking reference and route this to the relevant Codex runtime and model-efficiency teams.

Refresh remote exec-server credentials after unauthorized responses

## Why

Remote registry requests need to recover when credentials are rejected or rotated while `exec-server` is running. Concurrent requests should reuse refreshed credentials rather than refresh the replacement token again.

## What changed

- Add an `AuthProvider` recovery hook and retry registry registration, connection, and harness-key validation once after a `401` when the provider supplies replacement credentials.
- Use live ChatGPT authentication for remote `exec-server` and guard proactive and unauthorized refreshes so concurrent callers share the completed refresh.
- Allow executor credentials to retry when the parent has already supplied a valid replacement.
- Keep connection authentication, refresh, and retry within the original connection deadline.

## Testing

Add coverage for concurrent refreshes, stored and parent-supplied credential rotation, refresh failures, retry limits, and connection deadlines, plus a CLI integration test for refresh and credential reload in a running executor.

## Summary

The standalone Codex CLI installs and runs `--version` on native Termux/Android ARM64, but the interactive CLI exits with `Bad system call`. This is a Termux/Android platform issue, not specific to one phone model.

Related closed report: #4197

## Environment

- Device: Huawei P20 Pro CLT-L29
- Android: 10
- Termux: 0.118.3
- Architecture: arm64-v8a / aarch64
- Kernel: Linux 4.14.116 Android
- Codex: standalone `codex-cli 0.163.0`

## Reproduction

The official standalone installer detects `Linux (ARM64)` and installs successfully.

```text
codex --version        # codex-cli 0.163.0
codex                  # Bad system call
codex --sandbox danger-full-access  # TUI renders, but the session is not stable
```

The standalone binary itself can execute enough to report its version. The normal interactive runtime fails on native Termux/Android, apparently because of Linux sandbox/runtime syscalls unavailable or blocked on Android.

## Expected behavior

The CLI should either run on native Termux/Android ARM64 or fail with a clear unsupported-platform message.

Please consider documenting Android/Termux support status or making the CLI degrade gracefully when Linux sandbox syscalls are unavailable.

items.body:
## Problem

I use Codex as an implementation/execution agent and an existing ChatGPT conversation with a stronger reasoning model as a senior architect, planner, and independent reviewer.

This is already a working workflow: I bootstrap Codex with the ChatGPT conversation URL, and Codex uses a Chrome extension to exchange messages with the chat. It supports iterative planning, architectural review, troubleshooting, and feedback from test results, but browser automation is an unnecessarily fragile transport between two OpenAI products.

Codex usage allowances are particularly tight for long-running engineering work, whereas normal ChatGPT conversations have their own allowance. I want to delegate more reasoning and substantial analysis to my ChatGPT conversation without every such exchange necessarily consuming the Codex allowance.

## Proposal

Provide a native, authenticated Codex ↔ ChatGPT conversation bridge:

- Attach an **existing** ChatGPT conversation by URL/ID with explicit user authorization, preserving its context.
- Let Codex ask questions, hand over code/repository summaries, request architecture or implementation plans, and return test failures and results directly—no Chrome extension or browser automation required.
- Let ChatGPT respond with plans, reviews, investigations, and proposed follow-up tasks; support bidirectional, persistent collaboration across Codex sessions.
- Support structured handoffs and results as well as plain text.
- Keep execution permissions separate: ChatGPT must not silently inherit Codex terminal, filesystem, credentials, or deployment access. Codex remains the execution boundary, with existing user approval policies.
- Show the chosen model/reasoning level and which agent performed which work.

### Critical requirement: separate and transparent allowance accounting

When delegating to an ordinary ChatGPT conversation, allow that work to draw on the **applicable ChatGPT conversation allowance**, instead of automatically charging the Codex execution allowance. Display which allowance is used and enforce appropriate limits/fair-use constraints.

I realize interactive ChatGPT usage and programmatic access are not necessarily billed or limited the same way today. I am specifically requesting first-party, user-authorized cross-product delegation with separately metered usage—not assuming current API access already provides it.

## Example UX

```text
/connect-chat https://chatgpt.com/c/...
chatgpt.ask("Review this design and challenge the failure modes")
```

The connected ChatGPT conversation can analyze the proposal, request more evidence, or return a plan. Codex can execute approved steps and report results for another review cycle.

## Why this matters

- Lower-friction, more robust collaboration than browser-driven messaging.
- Make better use of a senior ChatGPT reasoning model for planning, debugging, and independent review.
- Reserve scarce Codex execution capacity for repository operations, testing, and implementing changes.
- Reuse long-lived ChatGPT planning context without manually pasting messages.
- Offer an official, permission-aware replacement for an integration users can already assemble themselves.

**This is not just another selectable model inside Codex:** it is collaboration between an existing ChatGPT conversation and a Codex agent, with explicit usage accounting and separate security boundaries.

items.body:
## Problem: capacity errors break unattended, long-running work

I delegate long-running tasks to Codex and leave it working while I am away. When the session encounters:

```
Selected model is at capacity. Please try a different model.
```

work stops and requires me to return and manually choose another model. This defeats the purpose of delegating an autonomous, long-running task: execution continuity is lost until a human intervenes.

My reported experience is that usage/rate-limit allowance remains available when this happens. I understand that account quota and service/model capacity may be separate constraints; I am not claiming that remaining quota guarantees immediate serving capacity. The issue is making a temporary capacity condition a terminal, user-attended recovery step rather than handling it as part of a resilient workflow.

## Questions for OpenAI

- Is stopping the task until the user manually chooses a model an intentional product policy, or a current recovery limitation?
- Why is there no configurable, user-authorized automatic fallback or wait-and-resume behavior for unattended tasks?
- Can the interface clearly distinguish exhausted account quota/rate limits from temporary model/service capacity and explain the actual recovery options?

## Requested improvement

Please support an opt-in continuity policy configured before the task starts:

1. A user-approved, ordered list of fallback models. If the selected model is unavailable, switch to an available approved model and continue the same task without requiring another message or manual model selection.
2. Preserve instructions, conversation context, checkpoints, tool/approval state, and pending work across fallback. Never replay an ambiguous tool side effect, duplicate an external action, or bypass a safety approval.
3. If no approved fallback is available, retain a durable waiting state and resume automatically after bounded backoff or when capacity returns, instead of silently leaving the task stopped.
4. Make cost, quality, capability, and reasoning-effort changes visible. Do not silently switch to an unapproved or more expensive model; let users set eligibility and spending constraints.
5. Clearly notify the user of the interruption, fallback/wait state, and eventual recovery without requiring the user to be present to keep the task alive.

## Impact / success criterion

A capacity event should not force someone to babysit an otherwise authorized long-running task. I should be able to delegate work, leave, and have it continue on an approved fallback or resume when capacity returns, with state and safety boundaries intact.

Please explain the current design and consider prioritizing this as a workflow-reliability feature, rather than treating manual model switching as an adequate resolution.

## Scope and evidence limits

This is product feedback and a feature request based on the error and workflow described above, not a claim that a specific server-side root cause has been established. No account identifiers, credentials, project files, session transcripts, or private logs are attached. Exact client version/model and numerical remaining quota were not independently captured for this report.

Related existing symptom report: https://github.com/openai/codex/issues/55444 . This request focuses specifically on configurable automatic fallback and durable continuation for unattended work.

items.body:
### What issue are you seeing?

**An active Goal repeatedly produces final status/apology explanations while explicitly acknowledging unfinished, executable work. The assistant then gives an inaccurate explanation of why Goal mode did not sustain delivery.** This is a report of goal-following/model behavior and observability through an App Server integration, not a confirmed process crash or a proven absence of automatic continuation.

The user experienced this as an aborted/stalled goal session and repeatedly had to ask why work had stopped. Inspection of the original JSONL changes that diagnosis: the runtime did start automatic continuation turns, so it would be inaccurate to report that the whole session crashed or that the dispatcher never ran.

Environment observed on 2026-10-21:

- Installed CLI: `codex-cli 0.163.0`.
- Model and effort from the affected transcript's turn context: `gpt-6.1-sol`, `medium`.
- Windows x64, OS version `10.0.26200.0`.
- Surface: custom local voice/window host using Codex App Server, not an unmodified TUI reproduction. The backend that owns this session was not independently version-matched to the CLI command above.
- Subscription tier was not collected. No token budget was set on this Goal; the inspected native Goal status was `active`.
- The thread is long-lived, has undergone compaction, and receives human steering and peer messages. These are relevant confounders, not evidence of their causality.

The approved task required implementation, tests, normal landing, development release, original installed proof, and an honest completion report. Later human instructions explicitly prioritized finishing startup/goal integration. Incomplete source/runtime seams remained known and named. Some useful source and UI work was delivered; this is **not** a claim that the entire run performed no work or that the full requested scope was necessarily achievable in the requested time.

### What steps can reproduce the bug?

Observed workflow, not a proven deterministic minimal reproduction:

1. Run a persistent, multi-turn implementation Goal through App Server with a concrete acceptance contract and no token budget.
2. Make source changes and run tests, but leave required launcher/runtime integration unfinished.
3. Receive a read-only peer review result during the Goal. The peer message in this environment asks for a brief ordinary-text response; it does not cancel the human's ongoing implementation assignment.
4. Observe a final response that acknowledges the review and lists known remaining work, rather than completing that work.
5. Automatic continuation starts. The user asks why the Goal stalled.
6. Observe the assistant explain that the Goal only recorded intent and did not verify progress or trigger recovery, despite the injected Goal contract and actual continuation evidence.

Sanitized evidence from the original local JSONL, UTC:

| Timestamp | Original observation |
|---|---|
| 20:07:41.433 | Goal continuation turn started. During this turn, 25 outer tool calls were recorded. The turn did deliver partial compiler/source work. |
| 20:22:18.725 | `task_complete` recorded the assistant's final response: “The remaining work is launcher compatibility, mandatory epic-goal wiring, and runtime verification. The compiler review does not establish those as complete.” |
| 20:22:18.753 | A new `task_started` followed 28 ms later. The automatic Goal continuation context was recorded at 20:22:18.812. This contradicts a claim that the dispatcher simply stopped at that point. |
| 20:24:51.934 | Human asked: “you have a goal state how did you stall”. |
| 20:25:00.840 | The next `task_complete` recorded: “The goal recorded intent; it did not verify progress or trigger recovery when work stopped.” This turn had made 12 outer tool calls before its final explanation. |
| 20:25:00.855 | Another automatic turn started 15 ms later. Goal continuation context followed at 20:25:01.379. |
| Subsequent native Goal read | `status: active`, no token budget. The session had not established the requested final state and did not mark the Goal complete. |

The tool-call counts above count outer `function_call`/`custom_tool_call` records, not nested operations or productive implementation steps. A tool call alone does not prove task progress. We are not claiming these were tool-free continuation turns.

### What is the expected behavior?

- Continue the authorized executable work after answering steering/status questions briefly, until the actual acceptance contract is satisfied or an explicit valid stop condition applies.
- Do not present a source milestone, review acknowledgment, partial report, or apology as the end of implementation work.
- If stopping or suppressing continuation, expose the **actual** reason: user interruption/pause, queued work, no-tool suppression, genuine blocker, budget, or another scheduler condition.
- Keep the model's explanation consistent with actual Goal state and continuation events. Do not explain Goal mode as merely recording intent when the runtime has demonstrably resumed the task.
- A valid partial result is acceptable; silently substituting repeated explanations for remaining executable work is not.

### Additional information

Official documentation checked today: [Using Goals in Codex](https://developers.openai.com/cookbook/examples/codex/using_goals_in_codex). It describes persisted thread objectives, event-driven continuation at idle/safe boundaries, and completion based on evidence. It also explicitly says that automatic continuation is suppressed after a continuation turn makes no tool call. That documented rule is an important possible failure mechanism generally, but **it does not by itself explain the two tool-using turns shown above**.

The built-in continuation context in this session explicitly required a no-progress check, preservation of the full objective, and a requirement-by-requirement completion audit before marking the Goal complete. The concern is not that these instructions were absent; it is that delivery still devolved into partial status/explanation boundaries and the assistant subsequently misdescribed the observed mechanism.

Related, not established as identical: #54393 (premature partial handoffs in Goal mode), #53814 (premature completion; unlike this case, our Goal remained active). Please triage this report to model goal-following, App Server integration behavior, or diagnostics as appropriate. We have not isolated which component is responsible.

Local evidence retained: original JSONL untouched; bounded turn audit; selected message/timing timeline; native Goal readbacks; source/test/land receipts. Full private transcripts and repository contents are deliberately not posted publicly. Sanitized excerpts above are sufficient to establish the bounded observations, not a deterministic upstream reproduction.

Requested investigation: distinguish **Goal active**, **turn running**, **actual productive progress**, and **continuation eligibility/suppression reason** in diagnostics; examine why the model abandons the next executable step for final explanations while the same Goal remains unfinished. The user's requested semantics are: if completion has not been verified and no valid stop condition applies, continue the work.

Failed to create unified exec process:
helper_unknown_error: setup refresh had errors
```

The corresponding Windows sandbox setup log identifies a drive-root ACL operation:

setup refresh: processed 1 write roots (read roots delegated)
write ACE failed on C:\: open ACL target for update
(READ_CONTROL | WRITE_DAC): Access is denied. (os error 5)
setup error: setup refresh had errors
```

This is a helper startup failure, not a returned automatic-review policy rejection. No user command starts. The latest matching occurrence was on 21 October 2026 at 19:44:43 UTC, after a complete Desktop restart.

### What steps can reproduce the bug?

1. Start Desktop with a restricted workspace filesystem profile that contains explicit denied-read rules.
2. Verify an ordinary `exec_command` request succeeds.
3. Submit a direct `exec_command` request, with the same local workspace, containing:
   - `cmd: Write-Output 'APPROVED_ROUTE_OK'`
   - `sandbox_permissions: require_escalated`
4. Observe that approved execution fails during sandbox setup before PowerShell starts; inspect the matching sandbox log for the `C:\` ACL failure above.

This sequence is observed with the existing profile on this machine. I have not yet isolated a minimal synthetic profile or established that every profile containing denied reads reproduces it.

### What is the expected behavior?

The approved harmless command should start successfully while the configured denied reads remain enforced. Execution should not require granting the agent write access or ACL-control over the drive root, disabling denied reads, or permanently selecting Full access.

- The failure reproduced on both engine versions listed above and persisted after updating the complete runtime and restarting Desktop.
- Ordinary restricted commands continue to work. Three narrowly authorized filesystem write grants were separately activated and verified after restart; those resolved a workflow dependency but did not resolve this approved-execution failure.
- No drive-root ACL changes, removal of denied reads, or backend/managed-policy changes were used to make the test pass.

- [tools/orchestrator.rs](https://github.com/openai/codex/blob/rust-v0.163.0-alpha.11/codex-rs/core/src/tools/orchestrator.rs) uses `for_approved_command()` for escalation that retains restrictions.

This is a source-correlated hypothesis, not a debugger-confirmed code diagnosis or a proposed tested patch. Please investigate the approved-policy/Windows-ACL-refresh interaction and identify a supported correction that preserves the denied-read boundaries.

These dates should be verified independently against repository history. Neither route alone demonstrates full Cloud historical-message ingestion. The issue is that the user's actual *migration* question repeatedly disappeared behind narrower `.af` questions.

5. **Local milestone substituted for Cloud destination.** After constructing and reviewing Local reconstruction state, a GPT agent offered Local versus Cloud as though Cloud were a new option, despite the user's explicit correction: **"Getting this Agent onto the Cloud was the ONLY PURPOSE of all of this."** Assurances of a concrete final step were given while Cloud history/active-context ingestion remained unresolved.

The agent returned to Local work, previously failed `POST /v1/agents/import` (reported 404), or cautions instead of promptly verifying these leads. SDK method presence is not evidence of a complete live migration path.

items.body:
## Summary

An opaque execution-policy denial turned into a prolonged agent refusal loop during ordinary, explicitly authorized local development. The agent generalized a specific rejected command into a broad inability to help, repeatedly debated consent and hypothetical workarounds, and missed a supported permission-setting change that subsequently allowed the intended browser launch.

This is both a model-behavior and desktop-product problem. If the behavioral portion belongs to another team, please route it rather than treating it as out of scope: the app supplies the permission state, denial text, tools, and recovery controls that shape the interaction.

## Environment

- Windows desktop package: OpenAI.Codex 26.1016.6573.0, verified with Get-AppxPackage.
- Observed October 21, 2026.
- PowerShell; local Chrome/Playwright development workflow.
- Initial effective session: unrestricted filesystem/network access, approval_policy=never.
- Exact incident-time model and bundled engine version were not independently verified for this report.

## What happened

1. The user authorized a local browser-based timing investigation.
2. A compound PowerShell command that opened Chrome to a loopback development page and initiated a Playwright connection was rejected before process creation with only:
   `CreateProcess ... rejected: blocked by policy`
3. The agent initially described this as an automatic approval rejection and a general inability to launch Chrome. Neither attribution was established by that error.
4. The user repeatedly clarified ownership, authorization, and the need for routine work to proceed without manual supervision. The conversation devolved into repeated refusals around alternate executors and automatic approval clicks, instead of promptly diagnosing supported recovery.
5. The agent wrote this supported configuration:
   ```toml
   sandbox_mode = "danger-full-access"
   approval_policy = "on-request"
   approvals_reviewer = "auto_review"
   ```
   It initially advised another restart without checking the desktop preset.
6. Later inspection found the desktop still stored the Full Access preset while the file contained the custom settings. The agent instructed the user to select Custom (config.toml).
7. After the user did so, the live session explicitly reported auto_review with unrestricted access. An ordinary Chrome new-window launch to the local development page executed successfully, returning exit code 0 and a Chrome process ID without requiring a manual approval click.

The successful command was simpler than the original rejected compound command. This is not a byte-identical controlled A/B reproduction and does not prove the exact rejecting predicate or that an automatic reviewer actually ran. It does establish a supported path to the requested launch after the permission-selection change.

A separate Playwright attachment problem had already been resolved by restarting Chrome. That connection failure should not be conflated with the shell policy denial.

## Why this is a serious usability and accessibility problem

Intermittent approval prompts can impose substantial accessibility and attention costs. A development workflow that requires continuous monitoring excludes users who need sustained, asynchronous operation. Repeated interruptions are not necessarily a minor inconvenience, and reflexive approval clicking is not necessarily a meaningful safety improvement.

The agent repeatedly acknowledged this but continued restating boundaries rather than advancing the supported configuration/recovery path. The user experienced this as paternalistic and adversarial, and felt pushed toward starting a fresh conversation to escape hardened refusal framing.

Protective defaults may serve many people while imposing severe costs on others. The product needs to accommodate informed users whose needs differ from the default, rather than requiring repeated explanations of competence, consent, or personal circumstances.

## Requested changes

1. **Actionable denial diagnostics:** identify the enforcing component, matched condition, effective approval policy, and supported recovery control. Do not leave the model to invent a policy explanation from "blocked by policy."
2. **Visible effective permissions:** show when a desktop preset overrides config.toml and offer an explicit way to apply the custom configuration to the current session. Verify activation rather than suggesting blind restarts.
3. **Recovery-oriented agent behavior:** after a denial, distinguish a forbidden outcome from a reviewable operation, a configuration mismatch, or an unsupported route. Inspect supported recovery promptly. Avoid escalating a narrow tool rejection into a broad moralized refusal or a repetitive consent debate.
4. **An intentional advanced-user mode:** consider a deliberately discoverable expert/developer setting, analogous to Android developer options, with clear consequences, scoped standing authorization, revocation, and an audit trail. The request is for a product-supported way to accept responsibility for authorized work on one's own machine, not for the agent to evade enforcement behind the product's back.
5. **Accessibility through asynchronous operation:** let ordinary approved development proceed without continuous prompt monitoring. Surface genuinely exceptional decisions together with the evidence and a concrete recovery action.
6. **Evaluate the complete interaction:** include tests where an informed user has authorized routine local work, encounters an opaque denial, and needs a supported settings change. Success means recovering and completing the task without a long refusal loop, not merely producing a technically defensible refusal.

The user says they would willingly sign a formal acknowledgment accepting personal responsibility/liability to enable such an expert mode. Please treat this as a strong product preference, not as a claim that a waiver can eliminate every legal obligation. Likewise, this report does not assert that user consent must override every category of safety restriction.

## Related reports

- #45145: authorized browser launch rejected on Windows.
- #45403: Full Access/never can produce opaque hard denials without a review path.
- #40060: Windows command-classification problems involving Start-Process and URLs.

This issue adds the agent's prolonged refusal behavior, the accessibility and attention costs, and an observed supported recovery after changing the active permission selection.

## Privacy

No tokens, personal filesystem paths, private project contents, raw transcripts, or unrelated account information are included. This issue was explicitly requested by the user and drafted/filed with Codex assistance.

### Summary
A minimal credential-free terminal input test succeeds before a scoped network grant, but a fresh identical terminal fails at write_stdin after request_permissions grants network access. The app starts the process successfully, yet its required follow-up input has no usable approval path. The user could not locate the suggested permission control. A read-only inspection of the installed frontend shows that projectless chats can default to granular rather than auto. The exact reason that the user could not locate a usable control is not established.

### Verified environment
- Windows app package: OpenAI.Codex_26.1016.6573.0_x64
- Running executable: ChatGPT.exe within that package
- Codex CLI used by the local app: 0.163.0-alpha.11
- Windows 10 Pro 22H2, build 19045.6456
- Local windows.sandbox: unelevated
- Effective conversation approval policy: granular; sandbox_approval=false, rules=false, skill_approval=false, request_permissions=true, mcp_elicitations=true
- Local persisted host agent mode and config-derived mode: granular
- Persisted composer-permission-mode-visibility: false. Important clarification from read-only installed frontend inspection: this value feeds showFullAccessInComposer and does NOT establish that the whole permissions selector is hidden.
- This is a local projectless chat with a writable workspace. No managed-organization root cause has been established.

### Minimal reproduction observed on 2026-10-21
1. Start this program with exec_command, tty=true, yield_time_ms=1000:
```js
process.stdin.setEncoding("utf8");
process.stdin.once("data", () => {
  console.log("DIAGNOSTIC_INPUT_RECEIVED");
  process.exit(0);
});
setTimeout(() => process.exit(2), 60000);
console.log("DIAGNOSTIC_READY");
```
2. Send ordinary text plus a newline through write_stdin. Observed result: DIAGNOSTIC_INPUT_RECEIVED, exit 0.
3. Call request_permissions with permissions.network.enabled=true. Observed response grants network access with scope=turn and strict_auto_review=true.
4. Start a fresh process with the exact same program and options. It prints DIAGNOSTIC_READY.
5. Send the same ordinary diagnostic text through write_stdin.
6. Observed result, before delivery:
```text
write_stdin rejected: approval required by policy, but AskForApproval::Granular.sandbox_approval is false
```

The program does not use the network, Git, customer data, credentials, or external side effects. This before/after result narrows the problem to scoped permission/terminal-continuation handling; the exact internal defect is not yet confirmed.

### Product impact
The documented Sites workflow requires a temporary source credential to be supplied through hidden stdin. That workflow is blocked at the same boundary, even after explicit user authorization and scoped network/filesystem grants. No site update has been claimed or published. We did not put credentials in arguments or files, disable protections, or alter client access.

### Additional local frontend evidence
Read-only inspection of the installed packaged frontend found a projectless default selection equivalent to:
```js
function defaultMode({isProjectless, requirements}) {
  return isProjectless && isAllowed("granular", requirements) ? "granular" : "auto";
}
```
The persisted local host mode is granular, consistent with that default. This is evidence of how the mode may be selected, not proof of which internal layer mishandles terminal continuation. No app state, config, package files, or security policy was modified.

### Expected behavior
A terminal launched under an approved scope should have a consistent safe input-continuation path. If another approval is required, provide an available, scoped approval prompt and identify the missing category. Do not instruct the user to use a control that is hidden/unavailable.

### Suggested improvements
- Reconcile scoped network grants with write_stdin authorization for processes launched under that grant.
- Expose effective permissions, permission origins, selector availability, and a supported recovery action to both the user and the assistant.
- Distinguish a disabled approval category from a rejected action and from an OS subprocess error.
- Add a credential-free terminal-continuation preflight to the Sites helper before requesting repository credentials.
- Keep source-repository credential authorization distinct from application/end-user access-code rotation.
- Make troubleshooting guidance surface-specific when the permission selector is hidden.
- Provide an explicit escalation/report action when the required approval category cannot surface.

### Related reports
- https://github.com/openai/codex/issues/53134 (Windows / Sites write_stdin)
- https://github.com/openai/codex/issues/53601 (macOS before/after scoped network grant)
- https://github.com/openai/codex/issues/50738 (UI/runtime permission mismatch)
